title: Authorities: customs and police
subtitle: clear customs, claim asylum, search warrant, undercover police
summary: Handle the vocabulary of borders and policing - entry regulations, spot checks, claiming asylum, search warrants and the different kinds of police squad.

lesson.heading: Arriving in a country
lesson.text: On arrival you show your passport or national identity card, possibly a **landing card** - a form with your personal details and date of arrival - and often a **customs declaration form**, showing how much money and what goods you are carrying. You may need a visa and a **vaccination certificate**, depending on **entry regulations**.

examples.text: Could you give me a **landing card** before we arrive, please?
You may have to fill in a **customs declaration form** before going through customs control.
You'll have to show a **vaccination certificate** for infectious diseases when you enter the country.
You'll need a visa; the **entry regulations** are very strict.

lesson.note: Entry regulations are the rules about who can enter a country and for how long.

lesson.heading: Checks at the border
lesson.text: Some passengers use **e-passport gates**, which use **facial recognition technology** - software that identifies a person from a visual image. Customs officers carry out **spot checks** (checks done as a sample, not on everyone) to find **banned or restricted goods** and to see that you have not gone over your **allowance**, the amount permitted by law.

examples.text: At the airport they use **facial recognition technology** to check the photo is of the person using the passport.
Customs officers carry out **spot checks** on people's baggage.
When you come into this country, the tobacco **allowance** is 200 cigarettes per person.

lesson.heading: Sniffer dogs, customs and asylum
lesson.text: Officers may use **sniffer dogs** or **detector dogs** to **detect** - find something hidden - drugs, cash or explosives. In most cases you have to **clear customs** at the **port of entry**, the airport or port where you first enter. Some passengers wish to be recognised as **refugees** and **claim asylum**.

examples.text: At the airport, the security guards had **sniffer dogs**.
You have to **clear customs** even if you are flying on within the country.
You have to fill in the **port of entry** in this box here.
People entering from war-torn countries often **claim asylum**.
examples.note: People who claim asylum this way are called asylum-seekers.

lesson.note: Refugees have escaped from their own country for political reasons; persecution is cruel treatment because of race, religion or political beliefs.

lesson.heading: Policing the streets
lesson.text: The police **enforce the law** - they make people obey it. An officer can **stop and search** you if there is a **suspicion** that you are carrying drugs, weapons or stolen property. Normally they cannot enter your home against your wishes without a **search warrant**, official permission from a judge or magistrate.

examples.text: It is a police officer's duty to do all he or she can to **enforce the law**.
There are restrictions on the powers the police have to **stop and search** people.
The police have had **suspicions** about the activities at that address for some time.
They cannot enter your home without a **search warrant**.

lesson.heading: Traffic and surveillance
lesson.text: Many roads have **safety cameras** or **speed cameras** to make sure people are not **exceeding the speed limit**. **Traffic wardens** issue **parking tickets**, with fines for illegal parking. The police also use **surveillance** techniques, including **CCTV** (closed-circuit television), to monitor public areas.

examples.text: Ella was fined for **exceeding** the speed limit.
**Traffic wardens** issue **parking tickets** for illegal parking.
**CCTV** is used to monitor town centres and airports.

lesson.heading: Other types of policing
rows: a name for the army and police working together
police who do not wear uniform
police working secretly, using a false identity
police specially trained to fight the illegal drug trade
police trained to discover and fight bribery and corruption
computer crime, including cyberterrorism and cyberwarfare
tricking people on the internet into giving up personal information, especially bank details

lesson.text: Police is a plural word: The police **are** trying to combat crime, not ~~the police is~~.

exercises.prompt: Match the words to form collocations about customs and policing.
An official stopped the man because a sniffer dog had ___ something in his suitcase.
exercises.explanation: To detect something is to find something hidden.

exercises.prompt: During the Civil War many ___ crossed the border into neighbouring countries.
exercises.explanation: Refugees are people who have escaped from their own country for political reasons.

exercises.prompt: Throughout the centuries many people have suffered ___ for their religious beliefs.
exercises.explanation: Persecution is cruel treatment because of race, religion or political beliefs.

exercises.prompt: Ella was fined for ___ the speed limit.
exercises.explanation: To exceed the speed limit is to go faster than the permitted speed.

exercises.prompt: It is a police officer's duty to do all he or she can to ___ the law.
exercises.explanation: To enforce the law is to make people obey it.

exercises.prompt: When you come into this country, the tobacco ___ is 200 cigarettes per person.
exercises.explanation: Your allowance is the amount of goods permitted by law.

exercises.prompt: People entering from war-torn countries often claim ___ to avoid political oppression at home.
exercises.explanation: To claim asylum is to request permission to stay in another country to avoid persecution back home.

exercises.prompt: What do we call a police officer who might try to infiltrate a group suspected of terrorism?
exercises.explanation: Undercover police work secretly, using a false identity.

exercises.prompt: What do we call police officers engaged in combating the dishonest use of public funds?
exercises.explanation: The anti-corruption squad is specially trained to discover and fight bribery and corruption.

exercises.prompt: What do we call the police and the army considered as a single body?
exercises.explanation: Security forces is often a name for the army and police working together.

exercises.statement: The police is trying to combat cybercrime.
exercises.explanation: Police is a plural word: The police are trying to combat cybercrime.

exercises.statement: Phishing means tricking people on the internet into giving up personal information such as bank account details.
exercises.explanation: Correct - phishing is one of the many kinds of cybercrime.

exercises.prompt: Does each item belong to customs and immigration, or to policing?
Put this sentence about police powers in order.
exercises.answer: A police officer can stop and search you if there is a suspicion
exercises.explanation: A suspicion is a belief that something may be the case.
